catalog_quote: 6. Long vowels which are the result of the deletion of an 'h' or a quick 'l' are written as two vowels. They are pronounced as long vowels, i.e. without a break in between: karahay --- karaay "frying pan" sulud --- suud "inside" 7. Double consonants are pronounced as long consonants: mallaw "later" kinno "when" Stress in Kalagan usually falls on the penultimate syllable: ísu "child" bóbay "woman" asáwa "spouse" magaláong "to speak" piyaglaóngan "words, language" [p. i:] Kalagan as spoken by the Muslim community of Davao Oriental is a member of the Southeastern Mindanao group of languages. Two other dialects are referred to as Kalagan, namely Tagakaulo-Kalagan of South Cotabato and Davao del Sur, and Kaagan-Kalagan of Davao del Sur. ... The Kalagan used in this book is based on the dialect which is spoken in the municipality of Tarragona, Davao Oriental.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable (all five illustrative words, 2-5 syllables long, are marked with penult stress); the hedge 'usually' implies some words are stressed elsewhere, but no exceptions or conditioning are given. The guide separately notes long vowels (from h/l deletion, written double: karaay, suud) and long consonants (mallaw, kinno) without saying how they interact with stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'usually'; no exceptional words, no weight or morphological conditioning stated. Kalagan entries in the body of the phrase book carry no accent marks, so exceptions cannot be recovered from the book.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation-form words in a learner's pronunciation guide; word-level statement, no phrase-level discussion. NOTE the sister-variety description Dawson 1958 (Tagakaulo area, Glottolog taga1268; saved here) analyses the system differently: 'Stress is nonphonemic, occurring on the ultimate syllable only' with phonemic, culminative penult vowel length carrying a rising pitch ('might be regarded as an accent phoneme') — i.e. the familiar Philippine penult-length-vs-final-prominence pattern; and Wendel & Hale 1978 for Kaagan Kalagan [kll] report contrastive stress within the last two syllables. Erkmann's 'usually penultimate' for Tarragona Kalagan may therefore be a simplification of a length/accent contrast; confidence kept at medium.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Erkmann/SIL phrase book) explicitly describes 'Kalagan as spoken by the Muslim community of Davao Oriental.. based on the dialect spoken in the municipality of Tarragona, Davao Oriental', which SIL's archive tags as Kalagan [kqe] and Glottolog lists under kala1388 — identity matches the target. The earlier scan's named source, Dawson 1958 'The phonemes of Kalagan', turned out to be online (archive.org Rosetta items filed under kqe) and was downloaded and read, but its fieldsite (Lumabat and Mainit rivers beyond Malungon, Cotabato) is the Tagakaulo area (Zorc 1977 Table 3 gives exactly this location for 'Tagakaolo'), and Glottolog files Dawson 1958 under taga1268 Tagakaulu Kalagan [klg]; Dawson himself notes his speakers 'do not distinguish Kalagan and Tagacaolo' but admit a speech difference from relatives near Digos. Dawson's final-stress-plus-phonemic-penult-length analysis should be credited to taga1268, not double-counted here (pointer left; Kaagan Kalagan [kll] (Wendel & Hale 1978, lexical stress) is already catalogued separately as kaga1255.

sources.citation: Wendel, Dag & Austin Hale. 1978 [1979]. Kaagan-Kalagan phonemic statement. Studies in Philippine Linguistics 2(1): 191-203.
sources.note: Describes Kaagan Kalagan [kll] (already catalogued as kaga1255): phonological word defined by primary stress; stress contrastive within last two syllables ('binit vs pi'nit), length derived from stress; rhythmic secondary stress. Different ISO language; not used for kqe.

sources.note: Second-hand: cites Kalagan lanut 'rice water' / la:nut 'abaca' as a length contrast; 'Stress is usually predictable (depending on the length or shortness of the penult vowel)'; Mansaka and Kalagan 'only have relics of proto accent'. Kalagan variety unspecified (data via SIL/Dawson).

sources.note: p. 54 sec. 4.1: 'Stress is nonphonemic, occurring on the ultimate syllable only. When the penultimate syllable is lengthened, there is also a nonphonemic rising pitch on this vowel, the final stress being less pronounced.' sec. 4.3: vowel length is phonemic (ga:bi 'taro' vs gabi 'night'), never more than once per word, 'Thus it might be regarded as an accent phoneme'; suffixes shift/remove root length. BUT fieldsite (p. 47) = Lumabat & Mainit rivers beyond Malungon, Cotabato = Tagakaulo area; Glottolog files this work under taga1268 Tagakaulu Kalagan [klg], not kala1388.

tone.quote: 1.2. THE PHONOLOGICAL WORD A phonological word may be represented by one syllable or by a sequence of syllables one of which carries stress. Words of one to eight syllables have been observed. However, unaffixed words do not have more than three syllables, and most commonly only two. Stress occurs on the ultimate or penultimate syllable with a preference of the penultimate position in two-syllable words. S ko "my" S'S batad "corn" 'SS tobag "answer" S'SS asawa "spouse" SS'SS magalaong "will say" [...] 1.2.1. LENGTH AND STRESS 1.2.1.1. Stress carries length in open syllables [...] 1.2.1.2. Stress in closed syllables does not carry length
tone.locator: typescript pp. [1]-[2], sec. 1.2 'The phonological word' and 1.2.1 'Length and stress' (stress under affixation: sec. 1.2.2)
tone.summary: No tone system is described anywhere in the 17 pages: word prosody is treated purely as stress (on the ultimate or penultimate syllable, penult preferred in disyllables) with vowel length as a concomitant of stress in open syllables; tone, pitch and intonation are never mentioned.
